etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English mowen (participle mowen), from Old English māwan (past tense mēow, past participle māwen), from Proto-West Germanic *māan, from Proto-Germanic *mēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to mow, reap”).

See also Dutch maaien, German mähen, Danish meje, Swedish meja; also Hittite [script needed] (ḫamešḫa, “spring/early summer”, literally “mowing time”), Latin metō (“I harvest, mow”), Ancient Greek ἀμάω (amáō, “I mow”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cut down grass or crops.
(transitive, often with through) To cut down or slaughter in great numbers.

quote.citation: 1915, Captain Robert Palmer, Letters from Mesopotamia:
quote.text: In the afternoon they attacked again, in close formation: our artillery mowed them, but they came on and on,  […]

quote.citation: 2019 March 6, Drachinifel, 25:58 from the start, in The Battle of Samar (Alternate History) - Bring on the Battleships!‎[1], archived from the original on 4 July 2022:
quote.text: On the one hand, we had a scenario where, effectively, the American admiral just went "You know what, all the destroyers attack", at which point they mowed through the Japanese destroyers like a Grim Reaper through a harvest of very, very dead gorn, especially with the Brooklyns in support.

definitions.definition: The act of mowing (a garden, grass, etc.).
(cricket) A shot played with a sweeping or scythe-like motion.

quote.text: I consider it would engender a stiff, tame, cautious mode of play, with only now and then a mow, or a chopping hit.
At times, they seemed to be playing an especially orgiastic version of Stick Cricket, all computerised mows over midwicket and 30 off the over.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mowe, from Middle French moue (“lip, pout”), from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”), from Proto-Germanic *mawwō (“muff, sleeve”). Akin to Middle Dutch mouwe (“protruding lip”). Doublet of moue ("pout").

definitions.definition: (now only dialectal) A scornful grimace; a wry face. [from 14th c.]

quote.text: Those that paint them dying […] delineate the prisoners spitting in their executioners faces, and making mowes at them.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:

1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: For every trifle are they set upon me: / Sometime like apes that mow and chatter at me, / And after bite me;

quote.citation: 1848, William Tyndale, edited by Henry Walter, Doctrinal Treatises and Introductions to Different Portions of the Holy Scriptures:
1894, Stanley J. Weyman, “Chapter III”, in Under the Red Robe:
quote.text: He mowed at me, and, bowing with ironical politeness, pointed to the house.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English mūga. Cognate with Norwegian muge (“heap, crowd, flock”).

definitions.definition: (now regional) A stack of hay, corn, beans or a barn for the storage of hay, corn, beans.
The place in a barn where hay or grain in the sheaf is stowed.
